item.title: Yemen's Houthis, Saudi-led coalition trade fresh strikes amid growing int'l concern
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12 08:19:00
Houthi supporters take part in an armed rally staged against the involvement of Türkiye and Pakistan with Saudi Arabia in Yemen's conflict, in Sanaa, Yemen, on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Mohammed Mohammed/Xinhua) Fighting between Yemen's Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition showed no sign of easing on Sunday as fresh attacks hit major airports in Saudi Arabia, while the Houthi group claimed new missile and drone operations against Saudi airports and energy facilities and the coalition vowed a firm response. Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said Sunday that a new attack on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh caused injuries. Earlier in the day, the Saudi-led coalition said an unknown projectile had struck a passenger terminal at the airport, and a fire resulting from the attack was being handled at the site. In a later statement, GACA said King Fahd International Airport near Dammam in the Eastern Province was attacked on Sunday evening, with damage assessments and safety inspections of the airport facilities underway. The Houthi group claimed it had carried out four missile and drone operations against airports and energy facilities across Saudi Arabia over the past 24 hours. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said the operations targeted King Khalid International Airport, King Fahd International Airport, and two facilities operated by Saudi energy giant Aramco. In a separate statement, Sarea warned that Saudi airports and airspace, except for the airports in the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina, remained "exposed to targeting" and constituted an area of operations for the group's forces. Meanwhile, Saudi airstrikes continued across Houthi-held areas in Yemen, as the Saudi-led coalition vowed to respond firmly to the Houthi strikes. Sarea claimed Saudi warplanes had carried out 124 strikes over the previous 24 hours targeting the capital Sanaa and the provinces of Taiz, Marib, Al-Jawf, Hajjah, Hodeidah and Saada. Houthi-run al-Masirah TV also reported earlier on Sunday that a Saudi airstrike hit Sanaa International Airport in Yemen's Houthi-held capital, with no immediate information on casualties or damage at the airport. A Yemeni military official told Xinhua that Saudi warplanes had launched intensive strikes on Houthi-controlled areas in the southwestern province of Taiz, where fierce fighting between government forces and the group has intensified. The escalating conflict has drawn growing international concern, particularly after a Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday killed 12 people and injured 309 others. "I am deeply shocked by and strongly condemn Saturday's lethal attack by the Houthis on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh," said United Nations (UN) Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, adding that attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure violate international law and "must cease immediately." The United Arab Emirates, Sudan, Egypt, Türkiye, Israel, Iraq, Syria, Palestine, Bahrain and the Arab League also condemned Saturday's attack. Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of the country's north. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government, now based in the southern port city of Aden. The renewed fighting marked a major escalation after a UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted major hostilities.

item.title: Exclusive: Zheng Qinwen 'hungry for more' after making China Open history, tells GT she finds her 'fire' back
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-12 01:12:00
Exclusive: Zheng Qinwen ‘hungry for more’ after making China Open history, tells GT she finds her ‘fire’ back By Lu Wenao Published: Oct 12, 2026 01:12 AM China’s Zheng Qinwen claims the women’s singles title at the 2026 China Open on October 11, 2026, defeating Russia’s Mirra Andreeva in the final. Playing in front of her home crowd, the Paris Olympic champion delivered a resilient performance to capture her maiden WTA 1000 title. Photo: Cui Meng/Global Times China’s tennis ace Zheng Qinwen said she was hungry for more achievements in her career after becoming the first Chinese player to win the China Open women's singles title on Sunday, describing the triumph as a first step toward realizing her potential. “I achieved something that I never achieved before when I was at my 21 years old. I was Olympic gold medalist, that's amazing, but still there's lot of things I never achieve yet. I want to achieve all of them,” Zheng told the Global Times after defeating fourth-seeded Russian Mirra Andreeva 7-5, 6-4 in the China Open women’s singles final. “I'm really happy I made the first steps. For me there's still more to come. I'm so hungry honestly for what's going to come in the next of my career because I know my potential, and I don't want to have a regret the day that I retire from tennis. I just want to give everything that I have in the tennis career.” The 23-year-old, who won Olympic gold at the Paris 2024 Games, claimed her first WTA 1000 title after a challenging period marked by an elbow injury and surgery in 2025. She said the victory represented another milestone after people repeatedly asked how she could surpass her achievements in 2024. “I know my potential, and I don't want to have a regret the day that I retire from tennis. I just want to give everything that I have in my tennis career,” she said. Zheng recalled how she struggled for around six months after returning from injury, at times feeling as though she had forgotten how to compete. The difficult period, however, taught her to cope with outside criticism and rediscover her motivation. “When I was at the lowest moment, everyone was saying I couldn't come back. Everyone had doubts about me,” she said. “Finally, after going through many losses, I found my fire again when I'm playing competitive matches.” “Tennis is not just about hitting the balls, it's also about how much you want to win,” she noted. The victory also carried special significance given her experience at last year's China Open, where elbow problems forced her to retire from her match against Czech player Linda Noskova. This time, she approached the tournament one match at a time rather than expecting to reach the final, let alone win the title. Across seven matches in 11 days, she said she had to contend not only with her opponents but also with her own doubts and weaknesses. “I need to be aggressive, but also need to control my errors. At critical moments, I cannot be soft,” Zheng said, adding that she was pleased to have taken her opportunities at crucial moments in Beijing. For Zheng, the experience of overcoming setbacks has also reshaped how she views a slump. She said she had initially expected her difficulties to last only a month or two, rather than six months. “I learned to coexist with myself, to not be disrupted by those voices. All of those things make me stronger,” she said.

item.title: Journey of a single pickup truck shows the value transition of 'In China, for the world': Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-11 23:57:00
Visitors gather at the 29th Chengdu International Auto Show held at the Western China International Expo City in Chengdu, Southwest China's Sichuan Province, on August 21, 2026. The 10-day fair covers an exhibition area of 220,000 square meters and brought together nearly 120 major domestic and international automobile brands, with about 1,600 vehicles on display. Photo: VCG The cross-border journey of a single pickup truck breaks the long-standing inertia of technology flowing "from West to East" and mirrors the profound reshaping of the global economic landscape. Today, "In China, for the world" has evolved into its version 2.0, with more products and technologies defined, developed, and manufactured in China serving global markets and helping foreign automakers catch the new wave of opportunities. It was reported that the Frontier Pro, the first model of Nissan designed, developed and manufactured in China for global export, will officially hit the Mexican market this month. It will later be rolled out progressively across Latin America, the Middle East, Australia and other markets. While the Frontier Pro is merely one specific example within the global industrial landscape, it reflects a plain truth: China today is no longer just an assembly line and sales market for multinationals, but also a source of global innovation and a joint creator of value. The phrase "In China, for the World" carries deeper and broader implications amid the high-quality development of China's economy. Nissan is not an isolated case in the global auto industry. Partnering with China's supply chain to go global amounts to securing a reliable "ticket for the voyage" - a consensus shared by a growing number of foreign automakers. SAIC-GM has extended its joint venture term by 20 years, with the Buick Electra E7 being shipped overseas from China. SAIC Volkswagen renewed its contract six years ahead of schedule and exports multiple vehicle models to Uzbekistan. Changan Mazda leverages its Nanjing plant to ship overseas variants of the EZ-6 to more than 20 countries and regions. China FAW Group, Toyota Motor Corporation and GAC Group, long-standing partners, have signed a new strategic cooperation framework agreement in Guangzhou. If "manufacturing capability" was one of the draws for foreign enterprises to set up roots in China, then China's "smart manufacturing capacity" gives their industrial upgrading and global footprint an extra boost. In the past, the mantra of "In China, for China" among major auto giants represented "exchanging technology for market access." The "In China, for the world" version 1.0 simply meant "Made in China, exported to the world." Today, however, "In China, for the world" has evolved into its version 2.0, with more products and technologies defined, developed, and manufactured in China serving global markets and helping foreign automakers catch the new wave of opportunities. This evolution means that the Chinese market has become an "innovation incubator" and "transformation accelerator," with China-foreign automotive cooperation entering a new phase where China's industrial chain feeds back into the global market. Innovation under the "In China, for the world" framework is not merely about multinationals ramping up investment to tap into China's innovation capability. More importantly, it fosters an "innovation ecosystem" in China where Chinese and foreign firms grow side by side. China boasts the world's largest new-energy vehicle market, the most complete industrial chain and the largest workforce of R&D personnel. Chinese manufacturing is shifting from "product export" to "technology export," and from "shipping goods overseas" to "exporting industrial ecosystems." It has achieved a historic leap from the one-way cycle of "China supplies, the world consumes" to two-way empowerment through "technology collaboration and ecosystem co-creation." The old one-way model of "market for technology" has been upgraded into a two-way partnership, with Chinese and foreign sides acting as mutual "technology partners." Modern joint ventures are no longer a simple grafting of production capacity, but instead represent deep integration between accumulated global technological expertise and China's innovative dynamism. According to statistics released by financial services firm UBS, since 2018, European automakers including Volkswagen, Stellantis, Mercedes-Benz Group and BMW Group have established technology partnerships with at least 38 Chinese companies and research institutions, covering areas such as software, hardware, batteries, and vehicle connectivity. Nissan has designated China as its global hub for innovation and exports. Volkswagen has built a full design-build-test-validate cycle in Hefei, dubbed "China's Wolfsburg." Renault, Porsche, Kia and others have all made choices aligned with this trend. Multinational automakers are unanimously repositioning China from a "sales destination" to an "R&D cradle" and "global export hub." This is a vote of confidence backed by real capital, and a clear verdict delivered by industrial logic. Facts have proven that China's new-energy industry never creates a zero-sum game where one side gains at the expense of the other; instead, it offers long-term opportunities for shared growth. The latest figures show that Tesla's Shanghai Gigafactory delivered more than 95,000 vehicles in September, hitting its highest monthly output this year. In the six and a half years since it went into operation, the Shanghai Gigafactory has produced over 4.5 million electric vehicles, accounting for more than 45 percent of Tesla's global output. China's vast market remains an opportunity for the world. Meanwhile, "international collaboration" and "technological innovation," as fast-growing components of China's development dividends, are being shared by more countries and enterprises across the globe. The automotive industry epitomizes economic globalization. The cross-border journey of a single pickup truck carries jobs, innovation and future prospects across industrial chains. It breaks the long-standing inertia of technology flowing "from West to East" and mirrors the profound reshaping of the global economic landscape. This new path of "In China, for the world" leads toward a greener, more efficient and inclusive tomorrow. If the world thrives, China will thrive, and if China thrives, the world will be even better. Noises that seek to swim against the tide and erect barriers will ultimately be repelled by irrefutable facts.

item.title: How Xiong'an's biggest waste facility is making one of city life's least-loved parts cleaner, smarter and almost invisible
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-11 23:01:00
The green ecological zone of Everbright Ecological Industrial Park in Xiong'an. Beneath it lies a waste treatment plant, adopting the "park on top, factory below" model. Photo: Courtesy of Everbright Ecological Industrial Park Two enormous steel claws swung slowly through the air, plunged into a mountain of garbage and rose again carrying huge loads of waste. From behind a glass wall, the scene looked almost like a giant claw machine - except that the "prizes" weighed tons and would soon be fed into an incinerator. What was more surprising was what people could not smell. There was no strong, unpleasant odor of garbage, no deafening mechanical roar and none of the grim industrial atmosphere one might associate with a waste treatment plant. Behind a control console, a technician moved two joysticks almost effortlessly, guiding the giant grab cranes back and forth across the waste bunker. Through the glass, the whole operation looked more like a scene from a science-fiction film. What surprised visitors even more was that there was a park right above the plant. People were walking along tree-lined paths, passing a lake and enjoying the green space, while Xiong'an's largest waste treatment facility was operating more than 20 meters beneath their feet. This is the Hebei Xiong'an Everbright Ecological Industrial Park, where Xiong'an's waste is being turned into electricity, heat and construction materials. The Global Times learned from the park's operator, the roughly 33-hectare complex adopts what its operators call a "park above, factory below" model. Its solid-waste facilities descend as deep as 27.5 meters underground, while more than 70 percent of the surface is landscaped with greenery. The facility can process 3,160 tons of waste a day and generate around 200 million kilowatt-hours of electricity annually, enough, according to the park, to meet the electricity needs of about 200,000 households. A technician remotely controls a rectangular grapple to grab waste via machine telemetry at the waste treatment plant at the Everbright Ecological Industrial Park in Xiong'an New Area on October 9, 2026. Photo: Hu Yuwei/GT A factory beneath a park For visitors, however, perhaps the first question is simpler: Where did the smell go? Zhang Xing, general manager of Hebei Xiong'an Everbright Ecological Industrial Park Co Ltd, told the Global Times that the answer works somewhat like giving the waste bunker a "super vacuum cleaner." Fans constantly draw air from the bunker into the incinerators, where it is used to support combustion. This keeps air pressure inside the bunker lower than outside, creating negative pressure. Fresh air can flow inward, but foul air is prevented from escaping. Garbage trucks are also isolated from the outside when they unload. They first enter a sealed transition chamber; only after the outer door closes can the inner door open. "So the odor cannot escape," Zhang explained. Noise is controlled just as carefully. Most of the plant's heavy machinery is located deep underground, where layers of earth and rock, along with the greenery above, act as natural sound barriers. Extra soundproof enclosures are installed around particularly noisy equipment, such as generators, to further reduce noise. The journey of a bag of household trash becomes even more revealing. Trucks first descend to an unloading platform eight meters underground. Waste is then stored in a bunker reaching 23 meters below ground, where it is left for about seven to 10 days before the huge crane grabs mix it and feed it into incinerators. There, temperatures exceed 900 C. A technician at the waste treatment plant monitors the flames inside the incinerator, where the flame temperature exceeds 900 C. Photo: Li Hao/GT The heat produces steam, which drives turbines to generate electricity. Part of that power is consumed by the park itself, while the remainder is fed into the grid. Zhang said the facility can save roughly 70,000 tons of standard coal. Even the material left after burning is given another life. Bottom ash is processed into recycled aggregate that can be used in municipal construction and road building. Residues from food waste, sludge and medical-waste treatment can be sent for incineration, while biogas produced in related processes is reused as supplementary fuel. Flue gas generated during incineration undergoes multi-stage purification before being discharged up to standard, Zhang told the Global Times. The plant's emission standards are stricter than both national and EU benchmarks. For instance, its dioxin emission concentration is only half of the limits set by China and the EU. All residual waste from the treatment of kitchen waste, sludge and medical waste is also sent to incinerators for harmless disposal. In a sense, the facility functions like the city's "stomach," taking in different kinds of waste, treating them safely, and turning what it can into useful resources. In the central digital control room, this circular system is translated into numbers. Boiler pressure, steam flow, steam temperature and other parameters flash continuously across a wall of screens. When a reading moves outside its normal range, an alarm identifies the corresponding system so operators can adjust the process or dispatch workers to inspect equipment. Boiler workshop at Everbright Ecological Industrial Park in Xiong'an New Area, North China's Hebei Province Photo: Li Hao/GT The digital control room offers a glimpse of a larger idea taking shape in Xiong'an: Environmental infrastructure does not have to sit at the edge of a city, hidden because residents would rather not see it. It can instead be technologically controlled, spatially integrated and, perhaps most importantly, designed as part of everyday urban life. One of the core innovations of this waste treatment plant is breaking the traditional layout of isolating waste facilities on urban fringes. Through sophisticated design, intelligent equipment and precise planning, the facility is fully integrated into the city's daily operation. Zhang told the Global Times that conventional waste treatment plants often raise public concerns over pollution and noise. To address such worries, the project adopted a de-industrialized, underground construction concept at the initial planning stage. Adopting the pioneering "park above, factory below" model, all operational facilities are built underground, with the deepest point reaching 27.5 meters below ground. The ground level is developed into an open ecological landscape park equipped with lakes and pedestrian trails. This concealed design eliminates visible industrial facilities, odor and noise pollution. What was once a concern for local residents has become a leisure spot, turning the urban waste infrastructure from a potential burden into an integral part of urban life. Street view of a large commercial complex in Xiong'an New Area, North China's Hebei Province, on October 11, 2026 Photo: Li Hao/GT 'Zero-waste city' That matters because Xiong'an itself is no ordinary Chinese city. Established in 2017 about 100 kilometers southwest of Beijing, Xiong'an New Area was designed to take on functions that are not essential to Beijing's role as the nation's capital, while exploring a new model of urban development. Its master plan describes the goal of building a green, intelligent and livable modern city, with ecological protection embedded in its development from the beginning. China launched the national "zero-waste city" pilot program in 2019, and 11 cities and five regions were selected to carry out the pilot work to curb urban solid waste. The pilot program, jointly led by the Ministry of Ecology and Environment and 17 other ministerial-level departments, aims to reduce waste generation at the source, cut landfill volume and boost resource recycling, according to the Xinhua News Agency. Xiong'an became one of China's first "zero-waste city" pilots in 2019. Here, "zero waste" does not literally mean producing no waste. It means minimizing waste generation, maximizing recycling and resource recovery, reducing landfill dependence and managing the remaining waste with the lowest possible environmental impact. Xiong'an has incorporated the concept into areas ranging from household and industrial waste to construction, agriculture and hazardous waste. In this "future city," household garbage is not the only waste being given a second life. At an environmental education center in Xiong'an's Rongdong area, visitors can see jars filled with recycled aggregates made from crushed and sorted construction waste, alongside bricks produced from recycled materials, Xinhua reported. The underground plant serves as the final stop in Xiong'an's waste management system. But treating waste is only the last step. If the plant is the city's "stomach," then its communities, schools, offices and businesses are like the cells of a living organism, working every day to produce less waste, sort what remains and keep resources in use. According to Xiong'an's official website, the new area has made zero-waste principles part of its urban planning from the outset, extending the approach beyond treatment plants to neighborhoods, construction sites, ecological restoration and public education. One key initiative is the creation of "zero-waste cells" - places where waste reduction becomes part of daily routines. More than 800 such sites have been established across 14 categories, including government offices, schools, residential communities, tourist attractions, supermarkets and hotels. In Wenhua community, for example, a team of more than 50 environmental volunteers helps promote everything from waste sorting to low-carbon travel. Residents now sort their garbage with an accuracy rate of over 85 percent, while the use of disposable paper cups and plastic tableware at community events has fallen by more than 70 percent. Technology is also making recycling easier and more rewarding. In the Jingyunting residential complex, smart recycling bins allow residents to scan a code, deposit recyclable materials and receive payments based on their weight. The rewards can be exchanged for cash or everyday goods. In just over a year, more than 350 households have registered, earning over 2,800 yuan ($390) in total, while two smart bins have collected 13 tons of recyclables. Across Xiong'an's newly developed residential areas, waste-sorting facilities now cover all communities, and 100 percent of household waste receives safe treatment, according to the local government. Residents deposit recyclables into smart recycling bins in a residential community of Handan, North China's Hebei Province, on July 29, 2026. Photo: VCG Chinese answer to a universal urban question This isn't just happening in China. From Copenhagen's CopenHill, where a waste-to-energy plant doubles as a ski slope and hiking destination, to Singapore's Tuas Nexus, designed to integrate solid waste and used water treatment while recovering energy and resources, cities around the world are experimenting with ways to make traditionally unpopular infrastructure cleaner, more efficient, and more closely connected to urban life. Seen in that global context, Xiong'an's underground plant offers a Chinese answer to a universal urban question: Can a city process what people throw away without sacrificing the environment in which they want to live? Back on the surface, the answer feels tangible. The giant steel claws are still moving underground. Incinerators are still burning. Turbines are still generating electricity. But above them, there is grass, water and a walking path. Therefore, perhaps the most striking part of Xiong'an's "zero-waste" experiment is not that the city has learned how to make garbage disappear. Instead, the experiment is about making the city's metabolism visible in a different way: Waste becomes energy, ash becomes building material, an industrial facility becomes public green space and infrastructure once associated with pollution becomes part of a neighborhood. For a world searching for greener forms of urbanization, that transformation may be the more important story hidden beneath the park.

item.title: How Belt and Road rail links redefine globalization for landlocked nations
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-11 23:00:00
The China-Laos Railway has completed four years of safe operations, carrying more than 62.5 million passenger trips and 72.5 million tons of cargo as of December 2, 2025. Photo: courtesy of China State Railway Group As of October 9, cumulative trade on the China-Laos Railway has passed 100 billion yuan (about $14.9 billion), with more than 20.77 million tons of import and export goods moved. In the first eight months of 2026, rail imports of Southeast Asian tropical fruits totaled 5.26 billion yuan, while exports of machinery and electrical products during the same period reached 7.42 billion yuan, up 58.4 percent year-on-year. Laos is the only landlocked country in Southeast Asia. With no coastline, all imports and exports must pass through neighboring ports and roads. That means higher freight costs, longer delays and more spoilage. The UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) estimates that landlocked developing countries face trade costs roughly 50 percent higher than their coastal peers. Of the 32 landlocked developing countries worldwide, 17 are also classified as least developed. Globalization over the past few decades has largely been driven by maritime trade. A landlocked country is inherently marginalized within that network. It is not that these countries fail to try; rather, the network was never designed to connect them. Laos used to be in exactly this position. Its goods had to leave through Thai or Vietnamese ports, leaving it with little say over price or timing. A farmer could expect to lose a fifth of his produce due to spoilage on the way to the port. A businessman importing equipment had to wait for a neighbor to clear customs. Geography had locked the country in, and the UN Development Programme has long listed Laos among the least developed countries. The railway changed that. The 1,035-kilometer line opened in December 2021. The fastest trains now run from Vientiane to Kunming in 9 hours and 36 minutes. The railway turned Laos from a country the network had forgotten about into a key node within it. It would be too simple to describe this as "China built Laos a railway." Laos has plugged into a new network whose nodes include Kunming, Vientiane, Bangkok and Kuala Lumpur, and which may one day reach Singapore. In this network, Laos has moved from the periphery to a hub. The figure of 100 billion yuan is not the most important part. What matters is the change in development logic behind it. In the past, a landlocked country had one route into global trade: borrowing a neighbor's port to reach the sea. It depended on that neighbor's ports, roads and customs, and every checkpoint added cost and uncertainty. Now railways, pipelines, digital networks and regional power grids are changing the fate of landlocked states. UNCTAD noted that landlocked developing countries have long accounted for less than 1 percent of global trade. However, that figure is starting to change, and the China-Laos Railway is one example. In Africa, the Addis Ababa-Djibouti Railway links landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti's port. In Central Asia, the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan Railway is still in the planning stages. These lines share one commonality: They are not simply opening a path to the sea; they are creating nodes, and those nodes provide many young people with opportunities they have never had. When Western media discuss the Belt and Road Initiative, they often ask whether it is a "debt trap." We believe that question points in the wrong direction. The real question is not who owes whom, but who has been connected. Laos has been connected. It has gone from "land-locked" to "land-linked." A trip from Vientiane to Kunming that once took days now takes under 10 hours. Durian spoilage has fallen from about 20 percent to approximately 5 percent. Young people who were once reluctant to work in factories now want to learn technical skills. When the road opens, goods move, people travel and technology spreads. Extensions of the line are already under construction, from Vientiane to Thailand and from Vientiane to Vung Ang port in Vietnam. Once these extensions are complete, Laos will be more than just land-linked. What matters even more is the direction of travel, both north and south. Durians go north, and electric vehicles go south, with people moving back and forth in between. The logic of globalization is shifting from being sea-driven to a combination of land and sea. For landlocked countries, this represents their first real opportunity.

item.title: Global mayors gather in Luoyang, discussing historic city's modernization path that preserves cultural roots
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-11 22:00:00
A foreign guest (right) at the 2026 Global Mayors Dialogue poses for a picture with his painting made while learning about local intangible cultural heritage in Luoyang, Central China's Henan Province, on October 11, 2026. Photo: VCG A spectacular 3D light show illuminates ancient city walls. Visitors take the wheel of a tractor. A giant hydraulic press at a manufacturing plant demonstrates the precision of China's heavy industry. These are some of the experiences awaiting international city chiefs in Luoyang, Central China's Henan Province, where the 2026 Global Mayors Dialogue opened over the weekend. More than 90 mayors or deputies, representatives of international organizations, and experts and scholars from over 10 countries, including China, the UK, Italy, Argentina and Algeria, took part in the event, exchanging views on cultural heritage preservation, industrial upgrading and urban renewal. The city's history has been a major draw. At the Longmen Grottoes and Luoyi Ancient City, mayors saw how Luoyang is preserving its cultural heritage while opening it up to visitors. Yun Sinang, deputy director of administration of Siem Reap, Cambodia, told the Global Times that she was impressed by the preservation of the grottoes, tourism facilities and improvements to the surrounding environment. Protecting cultural heritage helps showcase a country's identity to the world, she said, adding that she hopes more Cambodians will visit Luoyang to experience its culture and learn about its development. Luoyang, the capital of 13 dynasties in Chinese history, faces the challenge of protecting an extensive collection of heritage sites while continuing to develop as a modern city. Cultural heritage areas account for 52 percent of its main urban area. Measures such as conducting archaeological assessments before construction and adopting site-specific protection plans have helped the city accommodate urban development while safeguarding its historical legacy. Tourism has benefited from these efforts. Luoyang received 158 million tourists in 2025, generating more than 128.5 billion yuan ($19.2 billion) in tourism revenue, according to data provided to the Global Times. However, tourism is only part of the picture. Luoyang is also an established manufacturing center, known for products ranging from agricultural machinery and three-wheelers to heavy industrial equipment. Ahead of this year's F1 Shanghai race, British racing driver George Russell took a three-wheeler for a spin, and the clip grabbed attention on social media. But you may not know that Luoyang is a major production hub for three-wheelers sold worldwide. "They [Chinese three wheelers] are very famous in my country. They brought a lot of revolution. They are quite affordable. They have really modernized the way we move goods and people in our country," John Mahu Macharia, director of trade, Nakuru county, Kenya, told the Global Times. The city's industrial strengths also include high-end heavy equipment. During their visits, city leaders saw an 18,500-ton free-forging hydraulic press designed and manufactured with the participation of CITIC Heavy Industries. Among the world's largest and most advanced presses of its kind, the machine highlights the technological capabilities underpinning Luoyang's manufacturing sector. "We are very interested in Luoyang's work on new energy and technological development. Italy and Bologna are also working on these issues, but we still have much to learn. In Bologna, we are developing Tecnopolo, a new technology hub to support research and innovation, and we are keen to learn from other cities and explore new opportunities for cooperation," Francesco Leonardo Nelli, head of international relations of Bologna, Italy, told the Global Times on Saturday. For Yang Bokong, a tourism industry expert, the significance of Luoyang's development lies in how it brings heritage preservation and economic growth together. The city has moved beyond the perceived trade-off between protecting historical remains and developing industry. By breathing new life into cultural resources through immersive tourism experiences while upgrading advanced manufacturing, cities can make cultural inheritance and economic development mutually reinforcing, Yang said. The approach offers lessons for historic cities across the Global South, where local governments face the dual challenge of preserving cultural heritage and finding new sources of growth. Modernization need not come at the expense of history, Yang said. Luoyang's experience also points to opportunities for international cooperation in areas such as intelligent manufacturing, digital heritage preservation, urban governance and cultural tourism. European cities pursuing their own industrial and technological transitions are also looking for opportunities to exchange experience with Luoyang. Nelli told the Global Times on Saturday that he was particularly interested in Luoyang's work on new energy and technological development. "I think that there are a lot of technologies inside the high-quality products (in Luoyang). It is important to mix culture and tourism with the identity and functionality of this city," noted the mayor of Sesto San Giovanni in Italy, Roberto Di Stefano. Despite technological and industrial development, "the development of the city doesn't forget the history," Di Stefano stressed.

item.title: GT Voice: China's rapid progress in robotics offers South Korea opportunities
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-11 21:08:00
Illustration: Liu Xidan/GT The economic potential of humanoid robots extends beyond the machines themselves. The Chosun Daily reported on Sunday, citing Counterpoint Research, that demand for DRAM chips used in the "brains" of humanoid robots equipped with artificial intelligence (AI) is expected to grow more than 20-fold by 2030. The projected growth has raised hopes that humanoid robots could become a new source of growth for Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, top DRAM memory chipmakers in the world. As humanoid robotics quickly develops and progresses, China has established a substantial presence in this field. Chinese media outlets have reported that more than 140 Chinese companies were researching and developing humanoid robots in 2025, while a widely cited market study estimated that robots made in China accounted for 84.7 percent of global shipments last year. The growth of China's robotics sector creates massive opportunities for South Korean DRAM suppliers. Yet normal market competition with Chinese enterprises appears to be a concern in South Korea. In a separate article, The Chosun Daily reported that during the audit done by the country's National Assembly's Science, ICT, Broadcasting and Communications Committee on October 6, criticism was voiced that South Korea's investment in humanoid robotics lagged behind China's. And, two humanoid robots made by Chinese companies were brought to the audit to illustrate the gap between the two countries. The robots walked into the meeting room, shook hands with a representative and performed a dance. The demonstration offered a glimpse of South Korea's concerns about the gap in robotics development with China. China's advances in humanoid robotics offer greater opportunities for South Korean suppliers, but they appear to have raised concerns about the competitive gap too. Such mixed reactions reflect the complex responses that the rise of AI-driven smart industries can provoke. Today, humanoid robotics is emerging as a new frontier in AI development. The sector will create greater demand not only for robots but also for high-end chips, sensors and other electronic components the robots could rely on. Competition between China and South Korea seems to be inevitable, but it is only one part of a bigger picture. Humanoid robotics depends on a broad network of suppliers, creating opportunities for companies in the two countries to share at different stages of the supply chain. As China's industry expands, South Korean suppliers could find greater markets for their components. And, China and South Korea bring different strengths to the evolution of humanoid robotics. China's capabilities in robot manufacturing, supply-chain scale and real-world application scenarios provide a foundation for the industry's expansion. South Korea has accumulated expertise in semiconductors and electronic components used in these robots. The industry's growth could create more chances for greater complementarity, with expanding robot production potentially opening up additional markets for South Korean suppliers. The humanoid robotics sector is just one example. The same logic applies to the broader AI industry, where advances are creating new products, new applications and new markets. Therefore, China's technological progress need not be viewed by South Korea solely as a competitive challenge. Instead, it could open up new windows for broader bilateral cooperation. The greater potential for complementarity in high-end manufacturing is reflected in recent trade data. In September, South Korea's exports to China rose 122.7 percent to reach $26.01 billion, exceeding $20 billion for a fourth consecutive month. Semiconductors, wireless communication components and computers were among the main drivers of that growth. These figures point to growing demand in China for South Korean products, suggesting that the expansion of China's AI-related industries is creating greater opportunities for South Korean component manufacturers. As AI drives a new wave of high-end industrial development, South Korea's opportunity may lie not in viewing China's technological progress as a competitive challenge, but in finding ways to expand bilateral cooperation and share the greater benefits of cooperation.

item.title: Singapore award-winning documentary exposes historical truths of Unit 731 atrocities across Asia for global audience: Japanese scholar
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-11 18:55:00
People visit the Exhibition Hall of Evidences of Crime Committed by Unit 731 of the Japanese Imperial Army in Harbin, northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, Jan. 25, 2024. Photo: Xinhua A documentary revealing Japanese wartime atrocities, titled Inside Unit 731: Japan's Secret Human Experiments, produced by Singapore's mainstream English-language media outlet Channel NewsAsia (CNA), has received Singapore's national award for Best History Documentary at the 2026 Asian Academy Creative Awards (AACA) and has become a finalist for the 2026 AIBs in the international affairs documentary category. The AIBs (Association for International Broadcasting) results will be unveiled in London on November 20. As of press time, viewership of the documentary on YouTube has surpassed 1.45 million and continues to rise. The documentary crew traveled to locations including Harbin in Northeast China, conducting on‑site visits to the Unit 731 site, areas heavily affected by bacteriological warfare, and former Allied prisoner‑of‑war camps. They interviewed Chinese victims of bacteriological warfare, descendants of survivors from Allied prisoner‑of‑war camps, as well as scholars from the UK, the US, Japan, Singapore and other countries, exposing the heinous crimes against humanity perpetrated by Unit 731 during World War II, including bacteriological warfare and human experimentation. Issei Hironaka, an associate professor from Aichi Gakuin University in Japan who appears in the documentary, told the Global Times on Sunday that the documentary has won awards and drawn international attention due to its exposure of little-known historical facts, such as the development of biological weapons by the Japanese invading troops in Southeast Asia and other regions. People used to believe that the Unit 731‑led biological weapons development by the invading Japanese troops took place solely in China. However, the documentary reveals that Japanese forces committed these crimes in Southeast Asian nations as well, causing severe suffering to local populations, Hironaka said. These historical facts have greatly shocked numerous viewers, he said, adding that the significant attention to this documentary demonstrates the public's hunger for historical truth. The documentary is produced in English, targeting English‑speaking audiences who previously knew little about Unit 731 and Japan's wartime atrocities. It is reported that its Spanish‑language version is set to premiere on October 22 on Movistar Plus+, a major Spanish pay‑TV and streaming platform. According to Hironaka, exposing Japan's wartime crimes through multilingual content allows for the presentation of historical truths to global audience. In today's world, conflicts and armed hostilities continue to flare up, and the cruelty and folly of war speak for themselves. In the past, Japan waged wars in China and across Asia, inflicting profound disasters. To prevent historical tragedies from repeating themselves, it is imperative to clarify the historical facts of Japan's wartime aggression, conduct deep soul‑searching, and draw lessons for the future, Hironaka said. Nevertheless, the current Japanese government no longer talks about reflecting on that war. If this trend continues, Japan will struggle to maintain sound ties with victim countries in East Asia. Hironaka noted that the Japanese government must first sincerely face up to its wartime past and engage in soul‑searching as a perpetrator‑state.

item.title: China's Ministry of National Defense slams Lai's 'Double Ten' speech for hyping up 'mainland military threat,' pursuing 'Taiwan independence'
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-11 12:14:00
China's Ministry of National Defense China's Ministry of National Defense spokesperson on Sunday slammed Taiwan regional leader Lai Ching-te's so-called "Double Ten" speech for hyping up "mainland military threat" and pushing increased defense spending, saying Lai's remarks expose his attempt to seek "Taiwan independence" through military buildup and by soliciting external support. According to reports, Lai Ching-te recently delivered his so-called "Double Ten" speech, in which he hyped up claims that the Chinese mainland has continued to use military actions to pressure the Taiwan region and change the status quo across the Taiwan Straits, while calling for increased defense spending and stronger "whole-of-society defense resilience." In response, spokesperson Chen Xi said that there is only one China in the world, and Taiwan is part of China. This is the true status quo across the Taiwan Straits. Lai stubbornly clings to a "Taiwan independence" position, distorts right and wrong, hypes up the so-called "mainland military threat," and incites confrontation across the Straits. His attempts to seek "Taiwan independence" through military buildup and by soliciting external support.once again expose his nature as a source of trouble for Taiwan and a threat to peace, Chen said. In recent years, for their own partisan interests, the DPP authorities have pursued "independence" and resisted reunification, courted external forces, pushed so-called "whole-of-society mobilization" and attempted to turn the entire island into a battlefield. In doing so, they are tying the residents of Taiwan to the chariot of "Taiwan independence," undermining stability across the Taiwan Straits and sacrificing the Taiwan region's future, Chen said. The spokesperson noted that the PLA's regular exercises and training around the Taiwan island are aimed at deterring separatist moves for "Taiwan independence" and interference by external forces, and at safeguarding the security and well-being of residents in Taiwan. They are fully justified and beyond reproach. Chen said that "Taiwan independence" is fundamentally incompatible with peace across the Taiwan Straits. National reunification is an irresistible historical trend, a just cause and the aspiration of the people. We hope that Taiwan compatriots will fully recognize the extreme danger and harm posed by the Lai authorities' obstinate pursuit of "Taiwan independence," and join us in resolutely opposing "Taiwan independence" separatist forces and external interference, jointly safeguarding a peaceful and tranquil homeland and sharing the benefits and glory of national rejuvenation, Chen said. Global Times
